title: Writing Professional Emails in English
speaker: Oxford Online English
description: A comprehensive guide to writing clear, professional emails in English — structure, tone, and key phrases.
summary:
This Oxford Online English lesson covers everything needed to write effective, professional emails in English. The video addresses both structure and tone, which are the two most common areas where non-native speakers make mistakes in business email writing.

The lesson starts with *email structure*: a clear *subject line* that summarises the purpose, a proper *greeting* (Dear Mr Smith, Dear Sarah, Hi team), an *opening line* that establishes context, the *body* which contains the main message, a *closing statement*, and a *sign-off* (Kind regards, Best wishes, Yours sincerely).

A significant portion focuses on *tone* — the spectrum from very formal to informal, and how to judge which is appropriate. Key markers of formal tone include passive constructions ('It has been decided that...'), formal vocabulary ('I am writing to enquire about...'), and longer sentences. Informal markers include contractions, first names, and conversational phrases ('Just wanted to check in...').

*Opening formulas* are taught in detail: 'I am writing with regard to...', 'Further to our conversation last week...', 'Thank you for your email of 15th March...', 'I hope this email finds you well.' The video explains which situations call for which openers.

*Requesting and declining* are covered with politeness strategies: 'I would be grateful if you could...', 'Would it be possible to...', 'I'm afraid I am unable to attend...', 'Unfortunately, we are not in a position to...'

Common *email purposes* are practised through model emails: making a request, following up on a previous email, sharing information, apologising, confirming arrangements, and asking for clarification. Each model email is annotated with explanations of key phrases.

*Common mistakes* are highlighted throughout: reply-all disasters, unclear subject lines, too much background information, and abrupt endings. The lesson concludes with a checklist for reviewing emails before sending. Targets B1–B2 learners in professional contexts.

title: English for Meetings
speaker: Oxford Online English
description: Essential phrases and strategies for participating confidently in business meetings — from opening to decision-making.
summary:
This Oxford Online English lesson provides a comprehensive toolkit for participating in and leading business meetings in English. It is one of the most sought-after skills for professionals working in international environments.

The lesson opens by explaining the typical *structure of a meeting*: *opening*, *agenda*, *discussion*, *decisions*, *action points*, and *closing*. Understanding this structure helps participants anticipate what language will be needed at each stage.

*Opening a meeting* requires specific language: 'Shall we get started?', 'Let's begin with the first point on the agenda', 'We're here today to discuss...', 'We have a lot to cover, so let's keep things moving.' The lesson also covers how to set ground rules and introduce participants.

A large section covers *managing discussion* — how to *give your opinion* ('In my view...', 'I think we should...', 'My feeling is that...'), how to *agree* ('That's a good point', 'Absolutely', 'I couldn't agree more'), and how to *disagree politely* ('I see your point, but...', 'I'm not sure I agree with that', 'Have we considered...?').

*Interrupting and managing interruptions* are taught with phrases like 'Sorry to interrupt, but...', 'If I could just finish my thought...', and 'Let's hear what Maria has to say.' This is particularly valuable for learners who find it culturally difficult to speak up in meetings.

Keeping a meeting *on track* is covered with chairing language: 'Let's stay focused on the main issue', 'We're running short of time', 'Could we come back to that point?', 'Let's move on to the next item.'

*Clarifying and checking understanding*: 'Could you elaborate on that?', 'What exactly do you mean by...?', 'If I understand you correctly...', 'Could you say that again?'

The lesson ends with *closing a meeting* and summarising *action points*: 'To summarise what we've agreed...', 'Who's going to handle...?', 'Let's reconvene on Thursday.' Targets B1–B2 learners in professional settings.

title: Giving Presentations in English
speaker: Oxford Online English
description: How to structure and deliver a professional presentation in English — from opening hook to confident Q&A.
summary:
This Oxford Online English lesson teaches learners how to plan, structure, and deliver a confident presentation in English. The video is designed for professionals who need to present to colleagues, clients, or conference audiences in English as a second language.

The *structure* of an effective presentation is introduced as: *opening*, *overview*, *main body* (usually three main points), *conclusion*, and *Q&A*. Each section has its own language conventions, and understanding these gives speakers a reliable framework to follow under pressure.

*Opening a presentation* powerfully is given significant attention. The lesson teaches different opening techniques: a *surprising statistic* ('Did you know that...?'), a *rhetorical question* ('Have you ever wondered why...?'), a *short story* or *anecdote*, and a direct statement of purpose. Standard openers are also covered: 'Good morning everyone, my name is... and today I'm going to talk about...'

The *signposting language* that guides audiences through a presentation is central to the lesson: 'First, I'll cover... then I'll move on to... finally, I'll explain...', 'As you can see from this slide...', 'This brings me to my next point', 'To give you an example...', 'In summary...'

*Handling slides* is discussed: how to refer to visuals ('If you look at this graph, you can see...', 'The chart on the right shows...'), how to explain data ('This represents a 20% increase over...'), and how to keep slides simple.

Dealing with *nerves* and *mistakes* is addressed with practical strategies: speaking more slowly, pausing for emphasis, making eye contact, and recovering gracefully from errors ('Where was I? Right, so...').

The *Q&A section* is given a full segment: buying time ('That's a great question, let me think...'), redirecting ('That's slightly outside the scope of today's talk, but...'), and handling questions you don't know the answer to. Targets B1–B2 professionals.

title: Job Interview English
speaker: Oxford Online English
description: Prepare for job interviews in English — how to answer common questions, structure responses, and make a great impression.
summary:
This Oxford Online English lesson prepares learners for job interviews in English, covering the most common question types, effective answer structures, and the cultural norms of professional interviews in English-speaking workplaces.

The lesson begins with *preparation*: researching the company, understanding the role, and preparing *talking points* about your experience. Key vocabulary includes *CV* (or *résumé*), *cover letter*, *references*, *qualifications*, and *competencies*.

The *'Tell me about yourself'* question is given extended treatment as it is almost universally used as an opening. The lesson teaches a structured approach: current role → relevant experience → why you're here. Learners practise delivering a confident, concise 60-90 second answer.

*Competency-based questions* using the *STAR technique* (Situation, Task, Action, Result) are central to the lesson. Questions like 'Give me an example of a time you worked under pressure', 'Describe a challenging situation and how you handled it', and 'Tell me about a time you demonstrated leadership' are worked through with model answers.

*Discussing strengths and weaknesses* is covered with language for presenting yourself positively without sounding arrogant: 'One of my key strengths is...', 'I'm particularly good at...', 'An area I've been working to develop is...'

*Motivational questions* are addressed: 'Why do you want to work here?', 'Where do you see yourself in five years?', 'What attracted you to this role?' The lesson explains how to tailor answers to show genuine interest in the company.

Questions *at the end* of the interview are taught — the importance of having two or three thoughtful questions ready: 'What does success look like in this role?', 'What are the biggest challenges facing the team?'

*Tone and body language* are discussed alongside the verbal content. The lesson targets B1–B2 learners preparing for professional opportunities in English-speaking environments.

title: Networking in English
speaker: BBC Learning English
description: How to start conversations, introduce yourself professionally, and follow up at networking events in English.
summary:
This BBC Learning English lesson covers the art of professional *networking* in English — a skill many learners find particularly challenging because it requires spontaneous, semi-formal conversation in high-pressure social settings.

The lesson begins with the mindset of networking: it is about building *mutually beneficial relationships*, not just collecting business cards. Vocabulary introduced includes *conference*, *trade fair*, *industry event*, *mixer*, *colleague*, *contact*, *lead*, and *follow up*.

*Starting a conversation* with a stranger requires specific language. The video teaches natural openers for different contexts: 'Are you enjoying the conference?', 'Which company are you with?', 'Have you been to this event before?', and 'I saw your presentation earlier — I really enjoyed your point about...' The importance of *open questions* that invite longer responses is emphasised.

*Introducing yourself* in a networking context is different from formal introductions. The lesson covers the *elevator pitch*: a 30-second self-introduction that explains who you are, what you do, and what you're looking for. Model pitches are shown and dissected.

*Small talk* bridges gaps between professional topics. Topics considered safe for small talk in English-speaking professional cultures are introduced: travel, the event itself, current industry trends, and light personal topics. Topics to avoid are also flagged.

*Exchanging contact details*: 'Here's my card', 'Could I take your email?', 'Are you on LinkedIn?', 'I'll connect with you after the event.'

*Following up* after the event is covered with email templates: 'It was great to meet you at...', 'I really enjoyed our conversation about...', 'I'd love to continue the discussion over a call.'

The lesson targets B1–B2 learners in professional contexts, particularly those preparing for international conferences or working in multilingual teams.

title: Telephone English for Business
speaker: Oxford Online English
description: Master professional phone calls in English — making and receiving calls, leaving messages, and handling difficult conversations.
summary:
This Oxford Online English lesson addresses one of the most anxiety-inducing situations for non-native English speakers: making and receiving professional phone calls. Without visual cues and with the pressure of real-time response, telephone English requires specific preparation.

The lesson starts with the challenges of phone calls: no body language, potential for mishearing, accents, and background noise. Coping strategies are introduced early: asking people to speak more slowly, confirming key information by *repeating it back*, and not being embarrassed to ask for clarification.

*Answering the phone* professionally: 'Good morning, Apex Solutions, Sarah speaking. How can I help you?', 'Hello, this is James from...'

*Making a call* — getting through to the right person: 'Could I speak to the accounts department?', 'I'm calling to follow up on...', 'I'd like to make an appointment with...', 'Is this a good time to talk?'

*Taking and leaving messages* is given significant attention as this is a common scenario: 'I'm afraid he's not available at the moment. Can I take a message?', 'Could you ask her to call me back?', 'I'll make sure he gets the message.' The lesson teaches how to spell out names, give phone numbers slowly and clearly, and confirm message details.

*Being put on hold*: 'Please hold', 'I'll just transfer you', 'Your call is important to us', and the frustration of being transferred multiple times — with polite language for re-explaining your reason for calling.

*Difficult calls* — complaints, urgent requests, misunderstandings — are covered with language for staying calm and professional: 'I understand your frustration', 'Let me find out what happened', 'I'll personally make sure this is resolved today.'

*Closing a call*: 'Thanks for your help', 'I'll send the details over by email', 'I look forward to hearing from you.' The lesson targets B1–B2 learners in business contexts.

title: Negotiating in English
speaker: BBC Learning English
description: Key language and strategies for negotiating deals, salaries, and agreements in English.
summary:
This BBC Learning English lesson teaches the language and strategies needed for successful business *negotiations* in English. Negotiation is a skill that requires both linguistic precision and cultural awareness, and the lesson addresses both.

The video opens with the concept of *win-win negotiation* — the idea that the best outcomes leave both parties satisfied rather than one side winning at the other's expense. This framing influences the language used: collaborative rather than adversarial.

*Opening positions* are introduced with language that is firm but not aggressive: 'We're looking for a price of around...', 'Our preferred terms would be...', 'What we had in mind was...', 'We were hoping for something in the region of...'

*Making concessions* is a key negotiation skill: 'We could consider that if...', 'If you could meet us on price, we'd be willing to...', 'That might be possible, but only if...', 'We're prepared to be flexible on delivery times if...'

The language of *counter-offers*: 'That's a bit higher than we were expecting', 'We were thinking more along the lines of...', 'Could you come down a little on that?', 'Is there any room for movement?'

*Stalling and buying time*: 'I'd need to check with my team', 'I'm not authorised to agree to that without consulting my manager', 'Could we take a short break to discuss this?'

*Reaching agreement*: 'We have a deal', 'Let's shake on that', 'I think we can work with that', 'Subject to the written contract, we're in agreement.'

*Deadlock and walking away*: 'I'm afraid that's our final offer', 'We seem to have reached an impasse', 'Unless there's flexibility on your side, I don't think we can proceed.'

Cultural notes on negotiation styles in different English-speaking business cultures (UK, US, Australia) are included. Targets B1–B2 professionals.
